definition: Business process automation (BPA), also known as business automation, refers to the technology-enabled automation of business processes..
details: Business process automation (BPA), also known as business automation, refers to the technology-enabled automation of business processes.

explainer.lead: Business process automation uses software to carry out the steps of a business process, such as checking information, routing work, and recording completion. It matters because repeatable work can be handled more consistently, while people can focus on cases that need judgment.

tiers.eli5: It's letting software do the repetitive office steps, like paperwork, so people don't have to.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers automate repeatable workflows end to end, and a pitfall is automating a process before it is well understood.
tiers.paperLevel: Also called business automation; it refers to the technology-enabled automation of business processes.

explainer.example: When a supplier invoice arrives, software can start an invoice-handling process, extract or capture its details, check them against a purchase order, and route a matching invoice for payment approval. If the amounts disagree, the process can send the invoice to an employee for review instead of approving it automatically.
explainer.intuition: Many business activities follow a repeatable pattern: something arrives, information is checked, a decision is made, and the next step is triggered. BPA turns that pattern into software-driven work instead of relying on someone to coordinate every step by hand.
howItWorks: Define the process, including its starting event, activities, decisions, and desired result.
Configure software to detect the starting event and collect the required information.
Apply the process rules to perform activities or choose the next path.
Pass exceptional cases to people when the defined rules cannot resolve them.
Record progress and completion so the process can be tracked.
explainer.whyItMatters: BPA can reduce manual coordination and make repeatable processes easier to follow consistently. It also makes each step more visible, which can help organizations find delays and handle exceptions deliberately.
misconceptions: BPA is not automatically artificial intelligence; a process can be automated using ordinary software and defined rules.
BPA does not have to remove people from the process, because approvals and exceptions can remain manual.
Automating a poorly understood process does not itself fix the process.
